title: Radicals, nucleophiles and electrophiles
summary: Radicals form by homolytic fission and drive chain reactions such as alkane halogenation. Nucleophiles and electrophiles react by sharing electron pairs; at HL, Lewis acids and bases, SN1/SN2 and electrophilic addition and substitution mechanisms.

keyterms.definition: A species with an unpaired electron, shown with a dot (e.g. Cl•); highly reactive.
Breaking of a covalent bond so that each atom takes one electron, forming two radicals.
Breaking of a covalent bond so that one atom takes both electrons, forming a cation and an anion.
The three stages of a radical chain reaction: radicals form, react to regenerate radicals, then combine.
An electron-rich species with a lone pair that it donates to an electron-deficient carbon, e.g. OH⁻, NH₃, H₂O.
An electron-deficient species that accepts an electron pair, e.g. H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br₂ (polarized).
A reaction in which a nucleophile replaces a leaving group (such as a halide) on a carbon atom.
Reaction of an alkene in which an electrophile adds across the C=C bond.
Shows movement of an electron pair from a lone pair or bond to an atom or new bond.
A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair; a Lewis base donates one.
SN2: one step, rate = k[RX][Nu⁻], typical of primary halogenoalkanes. SN1: via a carbocation, rate = k[RX], typical of tertiary.
A positively charged carbon intermediate; stability: tertiary > secondary > primary.
In addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, H adds to the carbon with more H atoms, via the more stable carbocation.

questions.prompt: What is needed to start the reaction of methane with chlorine?
questions.explanation: UV supplies energy for homolytic fission of Cl–Cl (initiation).
Radicals are created from a molecule.

questions.statement: In a propagation step, a radical reacts and another radical is formed.
questions.explanation: e.g. CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl; the chain continues.
Termination removes radicals by pairing their electrons.

options: C–C and C–H bonds are strong and almost non-polar
questions.explanation: With no polar bonds or lone pairs, they do not attract nucleophiles or electrophiles.
Each atom keeps one electron, giving two radicals; heterolytic fission gives ions.

questions.text: A species with an unpaired electron is a ___.
questions.explanation: Radicals are shown with a dot and are very reactive.

questions.prompt: Why can the chlorination of methane give a mixture of products?
options: Cl• can also substitute into CH₃Cl, giving CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄
questions.explanation: Further substitution and termination steps give multiple products.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the radical chain mechanism.
questions.explanation: Initiation, two propagation steps, then termination.

questions.prompt: Which molecule is formed in a termination step of methane chlorination?
questions.explanation: Two methyl radicals combine to form ethane.
OH⁻ has lone pairs and a negative charge; it attacks electron-deficient carbon.

questions.statement: In a halogenoalkane, the carbon bonded to the halogen carries a partial positive charge.
questions.explanation: The halogen is more electronegative, making C δ+ and open to nucleophilic attack.
The hydroxide replaces bromine, which leaves as bromide ion.

questions.prompt: Ethene reacts with bromine water. What is observed?
questions.explanation: Electrophilic addition of Br₂ across C=C forms colourless 1,2-dibromoethane: a test for unsaturation.

questions.prompt: Match each reaction to its type.
questions.explanation: Reaction types follow from bond type and reagent.

questions.statement: A curly arrow shows the movement of a single electron.
questions.explanation: A full curly arrow shows a pair of electrons; a half-headed (fish-hook) arrow shows one.

questions.prompt: Which statement about electrophiles is correct?
questions.explanation: Electrophiles are attracted to electron-rich regions such as the C=C π bond.

questions.text: Heterolytic fission of H–Br produces H⁺ and ___.
questions.explanation: Br is more electronegative and takes both electrons.

questions.prompt: Order the steps when HBr adds to ethene.
items: C=C π electrons attack the δ+ H of HBr
questions.explanation: This is electrophilic addition via a carbocation intermediate.

questions.prompt: Which reagent and conditions convert ethene to ethanol?
options: Steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst, high T and p
questions.explanation: Hydration of alkenes is electrophilic addition of water.

questions.prompt: In BF₃ + NH₃ → F₃B–NH₃, BF₃ acts as a…
questions.explanation: BF₃ accepts the lone pair from NH₃ (Lewis base) forming a coordination bond.
Both donate an electron pair; "nucleophile" is used when the pair is donated to carbon.
Tertiary halides form a stable carbocation, and steric hindrance blocks back-side attack.

questions.text: The SN2 rate equation is rate = k[RX][___].
questions.explanation: Both species are in the single rate-determining step (bimolecular).
Polar protic solvents favour SN1; polar aprotic favour SN2.

questions.prompt: HBr adds to propene. The major product is…
questions.explanation: Markovnikov: H adds to CH₂, giving the more stable secondary carbocation, so Br bonds to C2.

questions.prompt: Order carbocations by stability, most stable first.
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups push electron density towards the positive carbon (positive inductive effect).

questions.statement: Benzene typically undergoes electrophilic addition rather than substitution.
questions.explanation: Substitution keeps the stable delocalized π system; e.g. nitration with NO₂⁺.

questions.text: In the nitration of benzene, the electrophile is ___.
questions.explanation: Concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates HNO₃, producing the nitronium ion.

questions.prompt: Which halogenoalkane reacts fastest with OH⁻ by SN2, other things being equal?
questions.explanation: The C–I bond is the weakest, so iodide is the best leaving group.
